title: Before the Cooking
bigQuestion: Why does a good meal start long before the stove is turned on?

story.title: A Dinner Planned on the Bus
story.kicker: Leo wanted to surprise his mom with dinner. The bus ride home was twenty minutes long. That was his planning time.
paragraphs: Leo's mom had worked late all week. On Friday, he decided to make dinner for her. Not a snack. A real dinner. He sat down on the school bus, pulled out a notebook and wrote one word at the top. Dinner. Then he stared at it. He did not know where to start.

His friend Amara leaned over. "What are you going to make?" Leo said spaghetti with sauce and a salad. "Okay," Amara said. "What do you already have at home?" Leo thought. There was pasta in the cupboard. Maybe. There was a jar of sauce. He was not sure about lettuce. "Then that is your first job," Amara said. "Check before you write your list."

Leo wrote Step 1: look in the cupboard and the fridge. Step 2: write the list of what is missing. Step 3: ask Aunt Rosa to take me to the store. Then he thought about time. His mom got home at six. Pasta took about ten minutes to boil. The water took another ten to heat. The salad took five. He wrote a time next to each step, starting from six and going backwards.

When he got home, he opened the cupboard. There was pasta, but only half a box. The sauce jar was there. The fridge had no lettuce, but it had carrots and a cucumber. He crossed lettuce off and wrote carrots. He did not need the store after all. He washed his hands for twenty seconds, got out the big pot, the cutting board and the colander, and lined them up on the counter.

At five-thirty, Aunt Rosa came in to help with the stove. Everything Leo needed was already out and ready. "You did the hard part on the bus," she said. At six, the door opened. Dinner was on the table, and the counter was almost clean.
story.think: Leo spent more time planning than cooking. Which of his planning steps saved him the most trouble later?

sections.title: Most of Cooking Is Not Cooking

lessons.title: Before, During and After
lessons.mainIdea: Cooking has three parts, and the part at the stove is usually the shortest.
reading: Picture a plate of scrambled eggs. The eggs cook in about three minutes. But think about all that happened first. Someone bought the eggs. Someone found the pan, the bowl and the fork. Someone cracked the eggs and whisked them. And after? Someone washed the pan and wiped the counter. The stove part was tiny.

Cooks call the three parts *planning*, cooking and *cleanup*. Planning is deciding what to make, checking what you have and getting things ready. Cooking is the heat. Cleanup is putting everything back the way it was. If you skip planning, you find out you have no eggs when the pan is already hot.

So a good cook plans first. Here is the rule. Most of cooking happens before and after the stove. Give those parts real time. A meal that is planned well feels calm. A meal that is not planned feels like a race.

words.d: deciding what to cook, checking what you have and getting everything ready before the heat goes on
the last part of cooking: washing, wiping and putting everything back in its place

look.title: Minutes in a Simple Breakfast (example)
look.cite: example times for one plate of scrambled eggs
look.prompt: How many minutes are not cooking? Which part is the shortest?

check.q: What are the three parts of cooking a meal?
check.why: Every meal has planning before, cooking in the middle and cleanup after.

check.q: Which part usually takes the least time?
check.why: The heat part is often only a few minutes. Planning and cleanup take longer.

check.q: A cook skips planning. What is most likely to happen?
choices: Something is missing when the pan is already hot
check.why: Without planning, you find out too late that an ingredient or a tool is missing.

lessons.title: Check the Cupboard First
lessons.mainIdea: Look at what you already have before you write a shopping list.
reading: Say you want to make grilled cheese. Do not write the list yet. Open the fridge. Is there cheese? How much? Is there butter? Open the bread bag. Count the slices. Two sandwiches need four slices. This step is called taking *inventory*. Inventory means a count of what you have on hand.

Write down what you find next to each thing the recipe needs. Bread: 6 slices, enough. Cheese: 2 slices, need 2 more. Butter: yes. Now the list writes itself. It only has the things that are missing. You do not buy a second loaf of bread you did not need.

Checking first saves money and space. It also stops waste. Food that gets bought twice often goes bad before it is eaten. Look at dates too. A carton of milk that is past its date should not go in the plan. Check, count, then list.

words.d: a count of what you already have on hand before you shop
already in your kitchen, ready to use

look.title: The Taco Night Check
look.text: The recipe needs 8 tortillas, 1 pound of ground beef, 1 cup of shredded cheese and a tomato. In the kitchen you find: a pack of 10 tortillas, no meat, a full bag of cheese and two tomatoes. There is also a can of beans nobody planned on.
look.prompt: What goes on the shopping list? What can stay off it?

check.q: What should you do before writing a shopping list?
check.why: Taking inventory first means the list only has what is missing.

check.q: A recipe needs 4 eggs. The carton has 2. What goes on the list?
check.why: You are short by 2 eggs, so eggs go on the list.

check.q: Why does checking first cut down on food waste?
choices: It makes food last longer in the fridge
You do not buy things you already have
check.why: Buying the same thing twice means one of them often goes bad before it is eaten.

lessons.title: Write the List by Section
lessons.mainIdea: A shopping list grouped by store section is faster to shop and easier to stick to.
reading: Stand at the front of a grocery store and look around. Produce is usually near the door. Milk and cheese are along the back wall. Cans and boxes fill the middle aisles. Frozen food is in its own cold row. If your list jumps from milk to apples to soup to cheese, you walk in circles.

So write the list in *sections*. Put all the fruits and vegetables together. Put the dairy items together. Put the cans and boxes together. Now you visit each part of the store once. It looks like this. Produce: carrots, cucumber. Dairy: cheese. Aisle: spaghetti.

The list has one more job. It keeps you from buying things you did not plan. A list is a promise to yourself. If it is not on the list, it waits for next time. That is how a list saves money and time in one move.

words.d: fresh fruits and vegetables, usually near the front of a grocery store
the parts of a store, like produce, dairy, frozen and the middle aisles

look.title: A Jumbled List
look.text: Here is Sam's list in the order he thought of it: milk, bananas, canned tomatoes, yogurt, spaghetti, apples, frozen peas, cheese, bread. The store has produce at the front, dairy at the back, aisles in the middle and frozen food at the far end.
look.prompt: Rewrite the list in sections so Sam visits each part of the store only once.

check.q: Which items belong in the same section of the list?
check.why: Apples and carrots are both produce, so they go together.

check.q: Why group a list by store section?
choices: You visit each part of the store once
check.why: A list in sections means no walking back and forth across the store.

check.q: Something looks tasty but is not on your list. What does a good shopper do?
choices: Rewrites the whole plan in the aisle
Puts back something from the list to make room
check.why: Sticking to the list keeps the plan and the money on track.

lessons.title: Start From the End
lessons.mainIdea: To plan a meal, start with the time you want to eat and count backwards through each step.
reading: Dinner is at 6:00. Baked potatoes take about 60 minutes in the oven. When do the potatoes go in? Count back. 6:00 minus 60 minutes is 5:00. The oven needs about 15 minutes to heat up first. So the oven goes on at 4:45. This is called *working backwards*. You start at the finish and count back to the start.

Do it for every part of the meal. The green beans take 10 minutes to steam. They go on at 5:50. Setting the table takes 5 minutes, so that happens at 5:45 while the beans wait. Write each step with its clock time on one sheet. Now you have a *timeline* for the whole meal.

The big idea is that different foods take different amounts of time. The slowest food sets the schedule. If you start the fast food first, it sits and gets cold. Find the longest job. Count back from dinner. Then fit the short jobs in around it.

words.d: starting from the time you want to eat and counting back to find when each step must start
a list of steps with a clock time next to each one

look.title: Cooking Times for a Simple Dinner (example)
look.prompt: Dinner is at 6:00. What time does each job start? Which job goes first?

check.q: Dinner is at 6:00. A dish takes 30 minutes. When should it start?
check.why: Count back 30 minutes from 6:00 to get 5:30.

check.q: Which food sets the schedule for the whole meal?
check.why: The food that takes longest decides when cooking must begin.

check.q: What happens if you cook the fastest food first?
choices: It sits and gets cold while the rest cooks
It cooks the other food faster
check.why: Fast food started first is done long before the slow food and cools off.

lessons.title: Everything in Its Place
lessons.mainIdea: Before you turn on any heat, get out and prepare every ingredient and tool you will need.
reading: Watch a cook on a cooking show. Little bowls sit in a row. One has chopped onion. One has grated cheese. One has the spices already measured. The cook never runs to the fridge in the middle. That setup has a French name, *mise en place*. It means everything in its place.

Here is how to do it at home. Read the recipe. Get out every tool it names: the pan, the spoon, the cutting board, the measuring cups. Then get out every ingredient. Measure what can be measured. Chop what can be chopped, with a grown-up for the knife. Line it all up in the order you will use it.

Why bother? Heat does not wait. If the onions are in the hot pan and you are still looking for the garlic, the onions burn. With everything ready, cooking is just adding things in order. It is calmer, safer and faster. Mise en place is the difference between a race and a plan.

words.d: a French phrase meaning everything in its place: all tools and ingredients out and ready before cooking starts
one food that goes into a recipe

look.title: The Counter Before Quesadillas
look.text: Nia is about to make quesadillas. On the counter she has: a pan, a spatula, a plate, four tortillas, a bowl of shredded cheese, and a small cup of sliced peppers. The stove is off. The butter is still in the fridge.
look.prompt: What is ready? What is not? What would happen if she turned on the pan right now?

check.q: What does mise en place mean?
check.why: Mise en place is French for everything in its place, all set out before the heat goes on.

check.q: When should ingredients be measured and chopped?
choices: Before the pan is turned on
check.why: Getting everything ready before the heat means nothing burns while you search.

check.q: What goes wrong when a cook looks for the garlic while onions are in a hot pan?
check.why: Heat does not wait. Food in a hot pan keeps cooking while you are away.

lessons.title: A Simple Day of Meals
lessons.mainIdea: A meal plan for one day lists breakfast, lunch, dinner and snacks, with something from each food group across the day.
reading: Take a piece of paper. Write Breakfast, Lunch, Snack, Dinner down the side. Now fill it in. Breakfast: oatmeal with banana and milk. Lunch: turkey sandwich, carrot sticks, an apple. Snack: yogurt. Dinner: rice, beans, sautéed peppers, and water to drink. That is a *meal plan* for one day.

Look at it with the five *food groups* in mind: fruits, vegetables, grains, protein foods and dairy. Across the day, did each group show up? Fruits: banana, apple. Vegetables: carrots, peppers. Grains: oatmeal, bread, rice. Protein: turkey, beans. Dairy: milk, yogurt. Yes. No single meal has to have everything. The whole day does.

A plan also helps the cupboard check. Every food on the plan goes on the inventory check, and anything missing goes on the list. Families eat many different foods, and that is fine. A plan just makes sure the day has variety and that nobody is hunting for dinner at six.

words.d: a written list of what will be eaten at each meal for a day or a week
fruits, vegetables, grains, protein foods and dairy

look.title: Check This Plan
look.text: Breakfast: toast with peanut butter, orange juice. Lunch: cheese pizza slice, grapes. Snack: crackers. Dinner: chicken, mashed potatoes, a roll. Drinks: water and milk with dinner.
look.prompt: Which of the five food groups shows up the least in this day? What could be added, and to which meal?

check.q: Which meal must have all five food groups?
check.why: Balance is measured across the day, not in every single meal.

check.q: Beans and turkey belong to which food group?
check.why: Beans, meat, eggs and nuts are protein foods.

check.q: How does a meal plan help with shopping?
choices: Every food on the plan can be checked and listed
It tells you which store is closest
check.why: The plan tells you what you need, so you can check it against what you have.

sections.title: Safe and Clean Before You Start

lessons.title: Hot, Sharp and Clean Hands
lessons.mainIdea: Before cooking, remember the three safety rules: hot things need mitts, sharp things need a grown-up, and hands need twenty seconds of soap.
reading: You are about to start. Stop and run the three rules. First, hot. Anything on the stove or in the oven can burn you, and hot metal looks the same as cold metal. Use a dry oven mitt or pot holder. Turn pot handles in, toward the back of the stove, so nobody bumps them. A grown-up runs the stove and oven.

Second, sharp. Knives, graters and can lids cut. A grown-up handles the sharp knife. You can use a butter knife on a cutting board for soft foods. Carry any knife point down at your side. Never try to catch one that falls. Step back and let it drop.

Third, clean. Wash your hands with soap and water for 20 seconds before you touch any food. Scrub the backs, between the fingers and under the nails. Tie back long hair. Wipe the counter. Now the kitchen is ready, and so are you.

words.d: a thick pad used to hold hot pans and lids
turning a pot's handle toward the back of the stove so it cannot be bumped

look.title: Spot the Problems
look.text: A pot of water is boiling with its handle sticking out over the edge of the stove. A sharp knife lies on the counter with the blade pointing at the edge. A cook grabs a wet dish towel to lift the pot lid. Nobody has washed their hands yet.
look.prompt: Name each problem you see and say what to do instead.

check.q: How long should you wash your hands before cooking?
check.why: The standard hand wash is 20 seconds with soap and water.

check.q: A knife slips off the counter. What should you do?
choices: Step back and let it fall
check.why: Never catch a falling knife. Step back and pick it up after it lands.

check.q: Why turn pot handles toward the back of the stove?
choices: So nobody bumps the pot and spills it
check.why: A handle sticking out can be knocked, spilling hot food on someone.

lessons.title: Washing Fruits and Vegetables
lessons.mainIdea: Rinse produce under cool running water and rub it with your hands, even if you will peel it.
reading: You have an apple, a bunch of grapes and a cucumber. Do not eat them yet. Fruits and vegetables travel from fields, trucks and shelves. They pick up dirt and germs on the way. Wash your hands first. Then hold the apple under cool *running water* and rub it all over with your hands. Do the same with the cucumber.

For grapes, pull them into small bunches and rinse them in a colander. Shake off the water. Firm produce like potatoes and carrots can be scrubbed with a clean vegetable brush. Leafy greens get rinsed leaf by leaf. Dry everything with a clean towel or paper towel. Drying rubs off even more.

Wash produce even if you will peel it, like an orange or a melon. The knife or your hands can carry dirt from the skin to the inside. Plain water is what to use. Soap is for hands, not food. Wash produce right before you use it, not days ahead, so it does not get soggy.

words.d: water flowing from the tap, which carries dirt away instead of leaving it in a bowl
a bowl full of holes that lets water drain out of food

look.title: Melon on the Counter
look.text: A cantaloupe just came home from the store. Its rind is rough and a little dusty. Marco says there is no need to wash it because nobody eats the rind. He picks up the knife and gets ready to cut.
look.prompt: Is Marco right? What could the knife carry from the outside to the inside?

check.q: What should you use to wash an apple?
choices: Cool running water and your hands
check.why: Rub produce under cool running water. Soap is for hands, not food.

check.q: Why wash a melon you are going to peel?
choices: So the knife does not carry dirt from the rind inside
To make it easier to cut
check.why: The knife touches the outside first and can carry dirt and germs into the fruit.

check.q: When is the best time to wash produce?
choices: A week before you use it
As soon as you get home, all at once
check.why: Washing right before use keeps produce from getting soggy in storage.

lessons.title: Read It All the Way Through
lessons.mainIdea: Read the whole recipe before you start so you know every tool, ingredient, time and step.
reading: Here is a recipe for banana muffins. A cook reads the title and starts mixing. Halfway down, the recipe says let the batter rest for 30 minutes. Dinner is in 40 minutes. Too late. Reading the recipe all the way through first would have caught that. It is the last planning step and the one people skip.

Read it with a pencil. Underline every tool: bowl, muffin pan, whisk. Circle every ingredient and its amount: 2 bananas, 1 cup of flour. Box every time: 30 minutes rest, bake 20 minutes at 350 °F. Now you know if you have the tools, the food and the time. If not, pick another recipe.

Reading first also shows the *order* of steps. Some recipes say to heat the oven first. Some say to mix the dry ingredients before the wet. Once you know the order, you can set up mise en place in that order. Then the cooking part is just following the line you already read.

words.d: how much a recipe makes, like 12 muffins or 4 servings
the sequence of steps, which matters because some things must happen first

look.title: Read Before You Mix
look.text: Recipe: Mix 1 cup oats, 1/2 cup peanut butter and 1/4 cup honey in a bowl. Chill 30 minutes. Roll into balls. Makes 12. Tools: bowl, spoon, measuring cups, plate. It is 3:00. Snack time is 3:20.
look.prompt: Can this snack be ready by 3:20? What in the recipe tells you?

check.q: When should you read a recipe all the way through?
check.why: Reading first tells you the tools, ingredients, times and order before you commit.

check.q: A recipe says chill 30 minutes. You have 15 minutes. What is the smart move?
check.why: Reading the times first lets you choose a recipe that fits the time you have.

check.q: What does the yield of a recipe tell you?
check.why: Yield is the amount a recipe makes, like 12 muffins.

review.q: Which part of cooking usually takes the shortest time?
review.why: The heat part is often just minutes; planning and cleanup take longer.

review.q: What is the first thing to do before writing a shopping list?
review.why: Taking inventory means the list only has what is really missing.

review.q: Dinner is at 6:00. The oven takes 15 minutes to heat and the dish bakes 45 minutes. When does the oven go on?
review.why: 45 plus 15 is 60 minutes. Count back one hour from 6:00 to 5:00.

choices: All tools and ingredients out and ready before the heat goes on
review.why: Mise en place means everything in its place before cooking starts.

review.q: Which two foods are in the same food group?
review.why: Oatmeal and bread are both grains.

review.q: How should pot handles sit on the stove?
review.why: Handles turned in cannot be bumped and spilled.

review.q: What is the right way to wash grapes?
choices: Rinse them in a colander under running water
Wipe them with a dry towel
review.why: Produce is rinsed under running water. Soap is for hands, not food.

review.q: Why read a recipe all the way through before starting?
choices: It makes the food taste better
You learn every tool, amount, time and step first
It is the last step of cleanup
The oven needs the time to heat
review.why: Reading first catches missing tools, missing food and steps that need extra time.
